terms.definition: The twisted, spiral-staircase shape formed by two DNA strands winding around each other.
terms.function: Lets two long complementary strands pack tightly and protect the base-pair sequence inside, while still allowing the molecule to unzip for copying and reading.
terms.whereItIs: The overall shape of the whole DNA model, visible along the outer curve of either strand.
terms.whyItMatters: The 3D twist is what lets an enormous length of DNA fit inside a nucleus far too small to see.

terms.definition: Two bases on opposite DNA strands that bond together — always A with T, or C with G.
terms.function: Holds the two strands together across the central axis and encodes the actual genetic information, via a fixed pairing rule that lets one strand template the other.
terms.whereItIs: The 'rungs' of the ladder, running the full height of the helix.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the part of DNA that actually carries information — the order of base pairs spells out genes.

terms.definition: The two outer rails of the DNA ladder, built from repeating sugar and phosphate molecules.
terms.function: Provides the structural rail that holds every base pair in place and gives each strand a consistent direction — it does not carry the genetic code itself.
terms.whereItIs: The two continuous outer strands running the full height of the helix.
terms.whyItMatters: Without the backbone, the base pairs would have nothing to anchor them into a stable, copyable molecule.

terms.definition: A specific segment of DNA sequence that contains the instructions for a particular protein or trait.
terms.function: Acts as a readable unit: the order of base pairs within a gene is transcribed into RNA and then translated into a protein.
terms.whereItIs: A contiguous run of consecutive base pairs along the strand; this model highlights one example region in the upper third of the helix.
terms.whyItMatters: Genes are the functional 'sentences' inside the DNA 'book' — inheritance, mutation, and traits all happen at the level of individual genes.

terms.definition: Where DNA is physically housed inside a cell: tightly coiled within the nucleus.
terms.function: Keeping DNA contained inside the nucleus protects it and separates the master copy of the genetic code from the rest of the cell's machinery.
terms.whereItIs: Inside the nucleus of almost every human cell (mature red blood cells are an exception — they lose their nucleus).
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding DNA's location explains why messenger RNA has to physically travel out of the nucleus to reach the ribosomes that build proteins.

terms.definition: The basic building block of DNA, made of a sugar, a phosphate, and one of four bases (A, T, C, or G).
terms.function: Nucleotides link together in long chains to form each DNA strand; the sequence of their bases is what encodes genetic information.
terms.whereItIs: Every position along both DNA strands — each backbone segment plus its attached base is one nucleotide.
terms.whyItMatters: DNA is often described as a 'chain of nucleotides' — understanding this building block explains both the backbone (sugar+phosphate) and the base pairs (the base) in one concept.

terms.definition: A tightly coiled package of DNA; humans typically have 23 pairs inside most cell nuclei.
terms.function: Organizes and protects an entire long DNA molecule by coiling it around proteins into a compact, manageable structure that can be copied and divided evenly during cell division.
terms.whereItIs: Inside the nucleus, most visible as X-shaped structures right before a cell divides.
terms.whyItMatters: Chromosome count and structure are how doctors detect certain genetic conditions (for example, an extra copy of chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome).

terms.definition: The two strands of a DNA molecule, which mirror each other exactly because of the fixed A-T / C-G pairing rule.
terms.function: Lets either strand act as a template to rebuild the other, which is the basis of how DNA copies itself before a cell divides.
terms.whereItIs: Both backbone strands together, considered as a matched pair across every base-pair rung.
terms.whyItMatters: Complementary strands are why a lab can determine an unknown DNA sequence just by reading its partner strand.
